steps.tx: An acute **elbow dislocation** ranks as the second most frequent large joint dislocation in adults, occurring with greatest incidence following high-energy falls on an extended, abducted arm. Over eighty percent involve posterolateral displacement of the radius and ulna relative to the distal humerus. The anterior joint capsule and medial collateral ligament tear sequentially as hyperextension leverages the olecranon.
steps.say: Elbow dislocation is the second most common major joint dislocation after the shoulder. Over eighty percent are posterolateral. A fall onto an outstretched hand drives the joint into hyperextension, tearing the anterior capsule and medial collateral ligament as the olecranon pops backward.

vis.title: Directional Patterns of Elbow Dislocation
rows: LCL complex followed by anterior capsule and MCL
LCL avulsion with coronoid anteromedial fracture
Direct violent blow to flexed olecranon
Extensive triceps and soft tissue disruption

steps.tx: Physical examination reveals gross **three-point disruption** of the elbow bony architecture. Unlike supracondylar fractures where landmark symmetry is preserved, the olecranon tip displaces markedly superiorly and posteriorly relative to the epicondylar line. The forearm appears visibly shortened, the elbow rests fixed in thirty degrees of painful flexion, and the distal humerus bulges prominently in the cubital fossa.
steps.say: On examination, the normal three-point relationship is completely destroyed. The olecranon tip rides high and posterior compared to the medial and lateral epicondyles. The forearm looks shortened, the elbow is held locked at thirty degrees flexion, and the distal humerus bulges in the antecubital fossa.

steps.tx: The **terrible triad** of the elbow represents a severe, inherently unstable injury complex combining posterior elbow dislocation, a radial head fracture, and an anteromedial coronoid process fracture. Disruption of both osseous stabilizers and the lateral collateral ligament complex leads to recurrent redislocation. Surgical reconstruction of the coronoid base, radial head arthroplasty, and lateral ligament repair are imperative.
steps.say: The terrible triad consists of an elbow dislocation combined with fractures of both the radial head and the coronoid process. Because both critical bone buttresses and lateral ligaments are destroyed, the joint is wildly unstable. Surgery to fix the coronoid, repair the radial head, and reconstruct the lateral ligament is mandatory.

vis.title: Terrible Triad Anatomy and Repair
rows: Lasso suture or lag screw through base
Resists varus and posterolateral rotatory laxity

steps.tx: Prompt **closed reduction** under adequate sedation or regional anesthesia should be executed without forceful jerking. The practitioner applies gentle longitudinal traction to the forearm while an assistant applies counter-traction to the upper arm. Downward pressure on the olecranon with gradual flexion safely disengages the coronoid process and slips the trochlea back into the olecranon notch.
steps.say: Reduce the dislocation promptly with steady inline traction on the forearm while an assistant holds the arm. Maintain traction, correct any sideways shift, and apply gentle forward pressure on the olecranon as you guide the elbow into flexion. It will click back into the trochlear notch smoothly.

right.title: Post-Reduction Check
points: Confirm distal radial and ulnar pulses
Check median and ulnar nerve sensation

steps.tx: Aggressive manipulation carries a formidable risk of **myositis ossificans** within the brachialis muscle bed. Clinicians must strictly forbid vigorous passive stretching, forceful massage, or prolonged immobilization beyond two weeks. After ten to fourteen days in a ninety-degree posterior splint, active protected motion is initiated to prevent debilitating flexion contracture while shielding healing collaterals.
steps.say: Never allow vigorous passive stretching or massage after reduction. Forcible stretching tears healing brachialis muscle fibers and provokes myositis ossificans, turning hematoma into bone. Keep the arm in a splint for only ten to fourteen days, then begin active, patient-guided motion.

vis.title: Complications and Prevention
rows: Early active motion at 10 to 14 days

quiz.q: Which anatomical triad defines the terrible triad of the elbow?
options: Elbow dislocation, radial head fracture, and coronoid fracture
Elbow dislocation, olecranon fracture, and capitellar shear
Supracondylar fracture, brachial artery tear, and median palsy
Radial head dislocation, ulnar shaft fracture, and PIN palsy
quiz.explain: The terrible triad of the elbow comprises posterior elbow dislocation, radial head fracture, and coronoid process fracture, causing severe joint instability.

quiz.q: Which intervention directly increases the risk of myositis ossificans following elbow dislocation?
options: Forceful passive stretching and deep massage
Early active elbow flexion exercises at 14 days
quiz.explain: Forceful passive manipulation and deep massage cause repeated micro-trauma and intramuscular haemorrhage in the torn brachialis, provoking heterotopic ossification.
